readerTitle: Your two best people have stopped talking. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (소매 체인 본사 안의 재고 보충팀) · 인물과 상황은 모두 설명용
insight: 팀원 간 갈등의 상당수는 성격 문제가 아니라 서로 부딪히는 목표와 불분명한 역할에서 시작된다. 사람을 고치기 전에 구조부터 본다.
misconception: 두 사람이 싸우면 성격이 안 맞는 것이니 누가 옳은지 정해 주거나 알아서 풀게 두면 된다.

sources.text: 팀 운영의 일반 원칙 (과업 갈등과 관계 갈등의 구분, 역할과 결정권 명확화)
모든 인물과 상황은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 시나리오 전체가 가상 사례입니다. 실제 연구 수치나 기업 사실은 쓰지 않았습니다. 과업 갈등과 관계 갈등의 구분은 일반적 개념으로만 소개했고, '과업 갈등은 항상 성과를 높인다' 같은 단정은 연구 결과가 엇갈리므로 쓰지 않았습니다.
테이크어웨이에서 결정 1~3을 각각 심리적 안전(PPL-05-01), 역할과 책임(PPL-05-03), 건강한 갈등(PPL-05-04)에 연결했습니다. 해당 레슨의 정의와 표현이 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your two best people have stopped talking. Now what?
body: Tom and Ana are the two strongest people on your team. This month they copy you on every email to each other.
Nobody has shouted. But the work is getting slower, and the rest of the team has started to tiptoe around them.

image.label: Two coworkers at separate desks, backs half-turned
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상 두 개가 등을 반쯤 돌린 채 놓여 있고, 두 사람 사이 공중에 'CC: Manager'가 적힌 이메일 봉투들이 쌓여 있음. 주변 동료들은 조심스럽게 지나감. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: You run stock replenishment for a retail chain.
body: Your small team sits in head office and decides what gets shipped from the warehouse to 60 stores.

**Tom** plans order quantities. Last month he cut them to bring stock levels down. **Ana** handles calls from stores. When shelves went empty, she started emailing the warehouse directly to raise Tom's orders.
Tom calls that going behind his back. Ana calls it doing her job. Both come to you on the same day.

image.label: Warehouse truck between head office and a store with empty shelves
image.brief: 가로 일러스트. 왼쪽 본사 사무실, 가운데 물류창고와 트럭, 오른쪽 일부 선반이 빈 매장. 본사에서 창고로 향하는 화살표가 두 갈래로 엇갈림(한쪽은 Tom, 한쪽은 Ana 색). 실제 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: What's your first move?
body: Each has told you their side in a few angry sentences. You have a busy week.

options.text: Tell them they're both professionals and should sort it out themselves
options.feedback: You save time today. But the overrides keep happening, and the conflict goes quiet instead of going away.

options.text: Meet each one alone first and ask for facts: which orders, which stores, what happened
options.feedback: It costs a day. You hear each side before they perform for each other, and each feels safe telling you the whole story.

options.text: Raise it at the weekly team meeting so everyone is aligned
options.feedback: It's transparent, but both now defend their positions in front of peers. Others start picking sides.

cards.title: Say you chose to meet each alone. Here's what you learn.
body: Tom: "Finance flags me every time stock runs high. That's my target." Ana: "Stores rate me on empty shelves. When Tom cuts, I get the calls."
Neither is lazy or careless. Their goals point in opposite directions. What next?

options.text: Decide which goal matters more and tell them both
options.feedback: Fast and clear. But one person simply loses, and next month a new clash will land on your desk again.

options.text: Bring them together, put both targets on the table, and agree who decides quantities and how exceptions get raised
options.feedback: It takes a harder conversation. In return, the fight moves from Tom versus Ana to both of them versus a shared problem.

options.text: Ask Ana to stop overriding, since ordering is Tom's job
options.feedback: It clarifies who owns ordering. But empty shelves are still a real problem, and Ana learns that raising it gets her shut down.

cards.title: Say you chose the joint meeting. Ten minutes in, it turns.
body: Ana says, "Honestly, Tom just doesn't care about the stores." Tom crosses his arms and goes quiet.

options.text: Let it run. Clearing the air will help
options.feedback: Venting can feel honest. But a debate about orders has become a verdict on Tom's character, and that is hard to take back.

options.text: Pause and steer back: "Let's stay with what happened. Which stores ran out, and when?"
options.feedback: You keep the disagreement and drop the attack. Tom can answer a fact. He can't answer a judgment about who he is.

options.text: End the meeting and speak to Ana privately about her tone
options.feedback: It protects Tom in the moment. But the problem stays unsolved, and both learn that disagreeing in front of you is dangerous.

cards.title: Say you chose to steer back. They found a deal.
body: Tom keeps ownership of order quantities. For the best-selling items, they agree a minimum shelf level that Tom's cuts can't go below.
Ana no longer emails the warehouse. She flags shortages to Tom, who must reply the same day. Both now read one shared weekly report showing stock levels and empty shelves side by side.
They aren't friends. They don't need to be. The CC emails stopped.

image.label: One shared report with two lines on the same chart
image.brief: 가로 인포그래픽. 하나의 주간 리포트 화면에 'Stock level'과 'Empty shelves' 두 선이 같은 차트에 그려져 있고, 그 앞에 Tom과 Ana가 나란히 서서 같은 화면을 봄. 실제 소프트웨어 로고 없음.

cards.title: Fight the problem, not the person.
body: A useful split: **task conflict** is disagreement about the work, like how much stock to order. **Relationship conflict** is friction about the people, like "he doesn't care."

Task conflict can improve decisions. Relationship conflict usually drains them. Many people clashes start as task conflict with a structural cause, such as goals that pull apart or no clear owner, and then turn personal when nobody fixes the structure.
cards.softwareNote: In a software company this often looks like sales measured on closed deals and engineering measured on stability. Sales promises a feature by Friday, engineering pushes back, and soon each side thinks the other is the problem.

cards.title: Not every clash is about structure.
body: Sometimes the goals are aligned and the roles are clear, and one person keeps acting badly. Then it's a performance issue, and treating it as a misunderstanding is unfair to the other person.
Also, don't become the messenger. Separate meetings are for listening. If you start carrying messages back and forth, you become part of the conflict and they never talk directly.

cards.title: Before fixing the people, check the goals and the roles.
body: Each decision in this story used an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1, listen alone first:** psychological safety. People tell the full story when it's safe to.
**Decision 2, settle who decides:** roles and accountability. Clear owners turn a feud into a shared problem.
**Decision 3, steer back to facts:** healthy conflict. Keep the disagreement, drop the attack.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** think of the last clash on your team. Write down what each person is measured on. Do those two numbers pull in opposite directions?
